data.text/markdown:
Mean, Variance, Skewness & Kurtosis

An interactive companion to DeepLearning.ai's Math for ML lesson. A distribution has a shape, and four numbers summarize most of it. Each one comes from a moment, which is the expected value of a power of the data:
# Statistic Formula Tells you about…
1 Mean ||(\mu||) ||(E[X]||) where the centre of mass is
2 Variance ||(\sigma^2||) ||(E[(X-\mu)^2]||) how spread out it is
3 Skewness ||(E\left[\left(\frac{X-\mu}{\sigma}\right)^3\right]||) asymmetry (which tail is longer)
4 Kurtosis ||(E\left[\left(\frac{X-\mu}{\sigma}\right)^4\right]||) how heavy the tails are
The odd powers (1, 3) keep the sign of a deviation, so they measure direction. The even powers (2, 4) discard the sign, so they measure size. Higher powers also give much more weight to points far from the mean. Drag, click and slide everything below. 👇

1 · The mean is a balance point

Think of each data point as a 1 kg weight on a seesaw. The seesaw only balances when the pivot sits at the mean, because that is where the deviations to the left and the right cancel out: ||[\sum_i (x_i-\mu) = 0||]Drag the weights (double-click the beam to add a weight, double-click a weight to remove it).

data.text/markdown:
2 · Variance: same mean, different risk

The lecture uses a game. You can win or lose $1 on a coin flip, or win or lose $100. Both games have an expected value of 0, yet they feel completely different. Variance measures that difference: ||[\operatorname{Var}(X) = E[(X-\mu)^2] = E[X^2] - \mu^2 \qquad \sigma = \sqrt{\operatorname{Var}(X)}||]We square the deviations so that negative ones cannot cancel positive ones. Use the sliders to compare two games.

3 · Skewness: which tail is longer?

Standardize first, ||(z = (x-\mu)/\sigma||), then average the cubes: ||[\text{skew} = E[z^3]||]Cubing keeps the sign and inflates large values. A long right tail produces a few huge positive cubes, so the skew is > 0. A long left tail does the opposite. For a symmetric shape the cubes cancel, so the skew is 0. A useful rule of thumb: in a right-skewed distribution, mean > median > mode. The mean is pulled toward the tail.

4 · Kurtosis: how heavy are the tails?

||[\text{kurtosis} = E[z^4] \qquad \text{excess kurtosis} = E[z^4] - 3||]The normal distribution has kurtosis 3, so people often report the excess above it. Every curve below has been standardized to mean 0 and variance 1, so it has the same centre and the same spread. Kurtosis is the remaining difference: how much probability sits far out in the tails. Click a legend entry to highlight a curve. Turn on the log scale to compare the tails directly.

5 · Sandbox: draw your own distribution

Click and drag across the bars to paint a probability distribution over the outcomes 0–20. Choose a preset to start from. The four moments are recomputed in Python every time you release the mouse.

data.text/html:
1. Draw a distribution with skewness ≈ 0 that is not symmetric. (Hint: it is possible!)
  2. Make the kurtosis as small as you can. Which shape wins? (Two equal spikes at the ends, which gives kurtosis 1, the theoretical minimum.)
  3. Keep the variance roughly constant and push the kurtosis above 6.
  4. Use Bimodal. Why is its kurtosis lower than the bell curve's, even though it has two peaks?

data.text/markdown:
Recap

Moment Power Sign kept? Unit Normal value
Mean 1 ✅ same as X μ
Variance 2 ❌ X² σ²
Skewness 3 ✅ unitless 0
Kurtosis 4 ❌ unitless 3 (excess 0)
  • Odd moments measure direction. Even moments measure magnitude.
  • Skewness and kurtosis are computed after standardizing, so they don't depend on units or scale and only describe shape.
  • Higher powers are more sensitive to outliers. This makes them informative about tails, and also noisy to estimate from small samples.
